yt_title: WSET Level 2 Grapes and Regions: the 15 Grapes You Must Know
yt_desc: WSET Level 2 Wines in one study session: the principal grapes, the regions where they make their best-known wines, and how a cool or warm climate changes their style. With maps, the regional grapes examiners love, the pairs students confuse, and a quick quiz at the end.

intro.title: The key grapes and *where they grow*
intro.sub: Principal grapes, their regions and styles, in one study session.
say: Most WSET Level 2 questions link three things: a grape, a region and a style. Learn those links, and you can answer a large part of the exam.
In this video we go through the principal grapes one by one: where they grow, what their wines taste like, and how a cool or a warm climate changes them. At the end, a quick quiz to check what stuck.

method.title: For every grape, learn three things
items: **Key regions**: where its best-known wines come from
**Typical style**: acidity, tannin, body and fruit
**Climate effect**: how cool and warm sites change it
say: For every grape, learn three things. First, its key regions: where its best-known wines come from.
Second, its typical style: acidity, tannin, body and the kind of fruit.
And third, how climate changes it. This last one is where many exam questions are hiding.

c1.title: Cool or warm climate?
c1.sub: The contrast behind many exam questions
say: Chapter one. Cool or warm climate?

climate.title: Same grape, two climates
climate.foot: Classic exam contrast: **Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon**.
say: A cool climate gives wines with higher acidity, a lighter body, and green or citrus fruit.
A warm climate gives riper fruit, more body and more alcohol.
Exam questions ask for exactly this contrast again and again, especially for Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon.

climate_regions.title: Cool, moderate or warm?
head: Climate
Typical regions
rows: Chablis, Champagne, Loire, Mosel, Marlborough, Central Otago, Oregon
Bordeaux, Côte d'Or, Northern Rhône, Rioja, Piedmont, Tuscany
Southern Rhône, Barossa, Napa, Central Valley (Chile), Douro
say: It also helps to sort the regions. Cool: Chablis, Champagne, the Loire, the Mosel, Marlborough, Central Otago and Oregon.
Moderate: Bordeaux, the Côte d'Or, the Northern Rhône, Rioja, Piedmont and Tuscany.

Warm: the Southern Rhône, the Barossa, Napa and Chile's Central Valley. But watch out: altitude and sea breezes can cool a warm country. Mendoza is cooled by height, and Casablanca in Chile by the Pacific.

c2.title: White grapes
c2.sub: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Grigio, Chenin Blanc
say: Chapter two. The white grapes.

chardonnay.title: Chardonnay
rows: Lean and mineral (cool) to tropical and oaked (warm)
Neutral grape: shows climate and oak clearly
say: Chardonnay is a fairly neutral grape, so it shows the influence of climate and winemaking very clearly. Its key regions: Chablis and the rest of Burgundy, California and Australia.

In Chablis, the coolest part of Burgundy, it gives lean wines with high acidity, green apple and lemon, usually with little or no new oak. In warm parts of California and Australia, it shows peach, melon and pineapple.
Many of those warm-climate wines combine malolactic conversion with new oak, for butter, vanilla and toast. And remember: Chardonnay is also one of the three main grapes of Champagne.

sauvignon.title: Sauvignon Blanc
rows: High acidity: grass, green pepper, gooseberry
say: Sauvignon Blanc is aromatic, with high acidity and green notes: grass, green pepper and gooseberry. It is usually fermented cool in stainless steel and drunk young.
In the Loire Valley, Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé give restrained, mineral, citrus styles.
Marlborough, in New Zealand, made it famous with a very intense, pungent style that adds passion fruit. In Bordeaux it is often blended with Sémillon, for dry whites and for sweet Sauternes.

riesling.title: Riesling
rows: Mosel, Alsace, Clare and Eden Valleys
Floral, citrus, high acidity; dry to sweet
Rarely oaked; ages to honey and toast
say: Riesling is very aromatic, floral and citrus, and it keeps high acidity even when ripe. It is rarely oaked, so the fruit stays pure.

In the Mosel, a cool German region with steep slate slopes along the river, it gives light, low-alcohol wines, from dry to lusciously sweet. Alsace and Australia's Clare and Eden Valleys make mostly dry, fuller styles; the Australian ones with lime.
Riesling ages very well, developing honey and toast, and it is used for late-harvest, noble rot and icewine sweet wines.

gris_chenin.title: Two grapes, many styles

cols.title: Pinot Grigio / Gris
items: **North-east Italy**: light, crisp, citrus and pear
The name on the label hints at the style

cols.title: Chenin Blanc
items: **South Africa**: fresh to rich, sometimes oaked

say: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape with two personalities. As Pinot Grigio in north-east Italy it is picked early for light, crisp whites with citrus and pear. As Pinot Gris in Alsace it is picked riper, for fuller wines with stone fruit. The name on the label is a strong hint.

Chenin Blanc has high acidity, which makes it extremely versatile. In the Loire, Vouvray comes in every style, from dry to sweet and sparkling, with apple, quince and honey. South Africa is the other key country.

c3.title: Black grapes
c3.sub: Pinot Noir, Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah, Grenache, Tempranillo, Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, Malbec
say: Chapter three. The black grapes.

pinot.title: Pinot Noir
rows: Pale, low to medium tannin, red fruit
Needs a cool climate; a Champagne grape
say: Pinot Noir has thin skins, so its wines are pale, with low to medium tannin and red fruit: strawberry, raspberry, cherry. With age it develops earthy and mushroom notes.
It needs a cool climate; in heat it loses its delicacy. Burgundy, especially the Côte de Nuits, is its reference region.
New Zealand, Oregon and the cooler parts of California and Chile make riper, fruitier versions. And it is a key grape in Champagne too.

bordeaux.title: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
items: **Cabernet Sauvignon**: deep colour, high tannin and acidity, blackcurrant
**Left Bank** (Médoc): warm gravel helps it ripen
say: Cabernet Sauvignon has small, thick-skinned grapes: deep colour, high tannin, high acidity and blackcurrant, sometimes with green pepper and mint. It needs warmth to ripen fully.
On Bordeaux's Left Bank, in the Médoc, gravel soils store heat and help it ripen. There it is blended with Merlot and other grapes.
Merlot ripens earlier and gives softer wines, with medium tannin and plum. One gives structure, the other gives flesh.

Merlot dominates the Right Bank, in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, where cooler clay soils suit it better. Outside Bordeaux, think of Cabernet from Napa Valley and Coonawarra, and fruity Merlot from Chile.

syrah_grenache.title: Syrah and Grenache

cols.title: Grenache / Garnacha
items: High alcohol, ripe red fruit, soft tannin

say: Syrah gives deep-coloured wines with black fruit. In the Northern Rhône, in Côte-Rôtie and Hermitage, it is structured, with black pepper. In Australia it is called Shiraz, and the warm Barossa Valley gives full-bodied wines with ripe blackberry, chocolate and sweet spice.

Grenache loves heat and drought: high alcohol, light colour, ripe red fruit and soft tannins. It is the backbone of Southern Rhône blends like Châteauneuf-du-Pape, with Syrah and Mourvèdre. In Spain, as Garnacha, it appears in Rioja and Navarra, and makes powerful reds in Priorat.

tempranillo.title: Tempranillo
rows: Red fruit, medium acidity and tannin
Loves oak: Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva
say: Tempranillo is Spain's leading quality black grape: medium to deep colour, red fruit, medium acidity and tannin.
In Rioja it is often blended with Garnacha; in Ribera del Duero the style is usually deeper and more concentrated.
It takes oak ageing very well. In Rioja, American oak brings vanilla and coconut, and you will see the ageing terms Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva.

italy.title: Sangiovese and Nebbiolo
items: Chianti, Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino
**Nebbiolo** (Piedmont): pale, yet very high tannin and acidity
Barolo, Barbaresco: cherry, roses, long ageing
say: Sangiovese is Tuscany's grape: high acidity, high tannin, and red cherry with herbal notes.
It is the main grape of Chianti and Chianti Classico, and Brunello di Montalcino is made from Sangiovese alone.
Nebbiolo, from Piedmont in north-west Italy, is a paradox: pale in colour, but very high in tannin and acidity.
Its two famous wines are Barolo and Barbaresco, with red cherry and roses that turn earthy over time. They need years of ageing to soften.

malbec.title: Malbec
rows: Deep colour, black fruit, medium to high tannin
say: Malbec gives deep-coloured wines with black fruit and medium to high tannin.
Its modern home is Mendoza, in Argentina, where high-altitude vineyards get sunny days and cool nights, keeping freshness and colour.
Its historic home is Cahors, in south-west France, where it gives firm, dark wines.

c4.title: Regional grapes often asked
c4.sub: One line each, and the pairs students confuse
say: Chapter four. The regional grapes that keep coming up.

regional_w.title: One line each
head: Grape
Where
Style clue
say: Albariño, from Rías Baixas in Spain: high acidity, peach and citrus. Grüner Veltliner, from Austria: citrus, green fruit and white pepper.
Furmint, from Tokaj in Hungary, famous for sweet noble rot wines. Torrontés, from Argentina: very floral and aromatic.
Gewurztraminer, from Alsace: lychee and rose, with low acidity. And Viognier, from Condrieu in the Northern Rhône: apricot, blossom and a full body.

regional_b.title: One line each
head: Grape
Where
Style clue
say: Gamay, in Beaujolais: light, red fruit, low tannin. Barbera, in Piedmont: high acidity and low tannin.
Carmenère, in Chile: black fruit with green pepper. Pinotage, in South Africa: a crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsault.
Zinfandel, in California: very ripe, high in alcohol, with jammy fruit. And Montepulciano, in Abruzzo: deep colour and soft tannin.

confused.title: Pairs students confuse
head: Easily confused
How to tell them apart
rows: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo / Vino Nobile di Montepulciano
A grape in Abruzzo / a Sangiovese wine from a Tuscan town
Same grape: cooler, peppery / riper, Australian
say: Some pairs are classic traps. Pouilly-Fumé is Loire Sauvignon Blanc; Pouilly-Fuissé is Chardonnay from the Mâconnais. Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is a grape in Abruzzo; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is a Sangiovese wine named after a Tuscan town.
Barolo is Nebbiolo from Piedmont; Brunello is Sangiovese from Tuscany. And Syrah and Shiraz are the same grape: the name usually signals a cooler, peppery style, or a riper Australian one.

c5.title: Quick quiz
c5.sub: Three questions. Pause the video if you need more time.
say: Chapter five. A quick quiz. Pause the video if you need more time.

q1.title: Barolo is made from which grape?
q1.expl: Barolo and Barbaresco: **Nebbiolo**, pale but very high in tannin and acidity.
say: Question one. Barolo is made from which grape? Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, or Barbera?
Nebbiolo. Pale in colour, but very high in tannin and acidity.

q2.title: A pungent Sauvignon Blanc with passion fruit most likely comes from…
q2.expl: **Marlborough**: intense, pungent, passion fruit on top of the green notes.
say: Question two. A pungent Sauvignon Blanc with passion fruit most likely comes from: Sancerre, Marlborough, or Bordeaux?
Marlborough, in New Zealand. Sancerre is more restrained, mineral and citrus.

q3.title: Which describes a cool-climate Chardonnay?
q3.expl: Cool climate: **higher acidity**, lighter body, green and citrus fruit. Think Chablis.
say: Question three. Which description fits a cool-climate Chardonnay?
High acidity, green apple and lemon. Think Chablis.

memorise.title: How to memorise them
items: Group the grapes by **colour** and by **climate**
Practise **both directions**: grape to region, region to grape
**Ten minutes** of mixed questions a day beats one long session
say: To make it stick: group the grapes by colour and by the climate they prefer.
Practise in both directions: from the grape to the region, and from the region back to the grape.
And ten minutes of mixed questions every day beats one long session.
